subsections.subsection_title: 1. What the OSCE station may say

items.text: Counsel a woman on the first day after caesarean delivery.
Provide discharge advice following an uncomplicated caesarean section.
Explain wound care and warning signs of infection.
Discuss pain relief and mobilisation.
Counsel a woman about preventing venous thromboembolism (VTE).
Help a mother who is struggling to breastfeed because of incisional pain.
Explain recovery time and when she can resume normal activities.
Counsel a woman about future pregnancies and mode of delivery.
Assess a woman who presents with fever, wound discharge or increasing abdominal pain after caesarean section.

blocks.text: Begin by introducing yourself, confirming the woman's identity and obtaining consent.
A suitable opening is:

"Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand that you have recently had a caesarean section. I would like to discuss your recovery, how to care for your wound, pain relief, feeding your baby and warning signs to watch for after discharge. Is that alright?"

items.text: When the caesarean section was performed.
Whether it was elective or emergency.
Whether there were any complications.
Whether the woman has fever, increasing pain, heavy bleeding or wound problems.
Whether she is mobilising, passing urine and tolerating food and fluids.
Whether she is breastfeeding and has adequate support.
Whether she has any history of blood clots or other relevant medical conditions.

blocks.text: Important: If she is acutely unwell, assess and stabilise her before continuing routine counselling.

subsections.subsection_title: 3. Explain what a caesarean section involves

blocks.text: A caesarean section is an operation in which the baby is delivered through surgical incisions in the abdominal wall and uterus.

Recovery involves healing of both the abdominal incision and the uterine incision. Mild incisional pain, fatigue and some vaginal bleeding are expected, but symptoms should generally improve rather than progressively worsen.
Explain that recovery varies between individuals. Many women need several weeks to recover comfortably, and recovery may take longer after an emergency procedure or when complications occur.

items.text: Keep the wound clean and follow the instructions given by the maternity team.
Wash hands before touching the wound.
Shower when permitted and gently clean the area with water and mild soap.
Pat the wound dry rather than rubbing it.
Avoid applying unprescribed creams, powders, herbs or antiseptics.
Wear loose, comfortable clothing that does not rub against the incision.
Follow instructions regarding dressings, staples, sutures and their removal.

blocks.text: Dressings should be managed according to the specific dressing type and local postoperative protocol.

blocks.title: Explain that she should seek medical assessment if she develops:

items.text: Increasing redness or warmth around the incision.
Increasing pain or swelling.
Pus or foul-smelling discharge.
Wound separation.
Fever or chills.
Increasing abdominal pain or feeling generally unwell.

blocks.text: A wound infection may require examination, wound sampling, antibiotics or drainage, depending on severity.

"Keep your wound clean and dry, and follow the dressing instructions provided by the hospital. Avoid applying unprescribed substances to the incision. If you notice spreading redness, increasing pain, pus, wound opening or fever, please seek medical attention promptly."
Pain is common after caesarean delivery, especially during the first few days. Adequate pain control helps the mother mobilise, sleep, care for her baby and breastfeed comfortably.

rows: Commonly used; generally compatible with breastfeeding at recommended doses
Useful for postoperative pain and inflammation if there are no contraindications
May be required for more severe pain; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration with monitoring
Spinal, epidural or wound-based techniques may form part of multimodal pain management

blocks.text: Check allergies, renal and hepatic function, bleeding risk, other medications and breastfeeding considerations before prescribing.

Avoid duplicate paracetamol-containing products and use opioids cautiously because of sedation and respiratory depression risks. Codeine is generally avoided during breastfeeding because of unpredictable conversion to morphine.

items.text: Support the abdomen with a pillow when coughing or changing position.
Use a comfortable breastfeeding position that does not place pressure on the incision.
Move slowly when getting out of bed.
Use prescribed analgesia before activities that are predictably painful.
Encourage adequate rest and assistance with infant care.

blocks.text: OSCE tip: Increasing or worsening pain, especially with fever, abdominal tenderness, wound changes or heavy bleeding, must not automatically be attributed to normal postoperative recovery.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Early mobilisation and prevention of venous thromboembolism

blocks.text: Caesarean delivery increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).

blocks.title: Once clinically safe, advise the woman to:

items.text: Sit up and stand with assistance initially.
Take short, frequent walks.
Perform gentle ankle and foot movements while resting.
Avoid prolonged periods of immobility.
Maintain adequate fluid intake unless fluid restriction is medically indicated.

blocks.text: Early mobilisation reduces immobility-related risk and supports recovery.

items.text: Previous DVT or pulmonary embolism.
Known thrombophilia.
Obesity.
Reduced mobility.
Emergency caesarean section.
Major haemorrhage or blood transfusion.
Severe infection.
Other significant medical or obstetric risk factors.

blocks.title: Depending on the woman's individual risk and bleeding status, prevention may include:

items.text: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), such as enoxaparin.
Intermittent pneumatic compression devices.
Other measures specified by the local obstetric protocol.

blocks.text: The drug, dose and duration depend on the risk assessment, renal function, body weight, bleeding risk and local guidelines. Some women require extended prophylaxis after discharge.
Do not prescribe anticoagulation automatically without assessing contraindications and the appropriate prophylaxis protocol.

content_groups.group_title: D. Warning signs of DVT and PE

blocks.text: Possible DVT

items.text: New unilateral leg swelling.
Calf or thigh pain and tenderness.
Unilateral warmth or redness.

blocks.text: Possible pulmonary embolism

items.text: Sudden shortness of breath.
Chest pain, particularly on breathing.
Coughing up blood.
Collapse, fainting or severe dizziness.

blocks.text: Suspected PE requires emergency assessment. Do not advise the patient to wait for a routine appointment.
A caesarean section does not usually prevent breastfeeding. Encourage early skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding when the mother and baby are stable.

items.text: Football hold: The baby is positioned beside the mother, away from the abdominal incision.
Side-lying position: May reduce pressure on the wound, provided the mother is alert and the baby can be positioned safely.
Supported cradle hold: Use pillows to support the arms and keep pressure off the incision.

blocks.text: A mother who has received sedating medication should not breastfeed or hold the baby without appropriate assistance if she is too drowsy to do so safely.
Milk production may be affected temporarily by delayed initiation, maternal illness, separation from the baby or ineffective feeding.

items.text: Offer feeds in response to the baby's hunger cues.
Seek help with positioning and attachment.
Express breast milk if separation or ineffective feeding prevents adequate milk removal.
Obtain prompt help if the baby is lethargic, feeding poorly or producing fewer wet nappies than expected.

blocks.text: Most commonly used postoperative medicines are compatible with breastfeeding, but individual drugs must be checked. Pay particular attention to opioids, sedatives and any medicines prescribed for complications.
Explain that vaginal bleeding, known as lochia, is expected after both vaginal and caesarean delivery because the uterus is healing at the placental site.
Lochia typically changes from red to brownish and then lighter in colour over the following weeks, although duration varies.

blocks.title: Advise the mother to seek urgent assessment for:

items.text: Sudden heavy bleeding or rapidly soaking pads.
Large clots accompanied by heavy bleeding or feeling unwell.
Dizziness, fainting or marked weakness.
Fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge or increasing pelvic pain.

blocks.text: A caesarean section does not eliminate the risk of postpartum haemorrhage or uterine infection.
After caesarean delivery, the catheter is generally removed when clinically appropriate, according to the postoperative plan.

items.text: Difficulty passing urine.
Painful urination.
Inability to empty the bladder.
Lower abdominal discomfort with inability to urinate.

blocks.text: Urinary retention and urinary tract infection may require assessment and treatment.
Constipation may occur because of reduced mobility, dehydration, iron supplements and opioid analgesics.

items.text: Drink adequate fluids unless medically restricted.
Eat fibre-containing foods such as vegetables, fruits and whole grains.
Mobilise regularly.
Avoid straining excessively.
Use a suitable stool softener or laxative if prescribed.

blocks.text: Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, marked distension or inability to pass stool or wind requires medical assessment.

items.text: Protein for tissue repair.
Iron-rich foods, particularly after significant blood loss.
Vegetables, fruits and whole grains.
Adequate fluids.
Sufficient energy to support recovery and breastfeeding.

blocks.text: Iron supplementation may be required after anaemia or postpartum haemorrhage, guided by the clinical assessment.

Encourage the mother to rest when possible and accept practical help with cooking, household tasks and infant care. Complete avoidance of activity is not recommended; gradual mobilisation is important.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Physical activity and return to normal activities

blocks.text: Recovery is gradual. Advise the patient to increase activity according to comfort and the advice of her surgical team.

items.text: Take short, regular walks as tolerated.
Avoid strenuous exercise and heavy lifting.
Keep the wound clean and monitor for complications.
Ask for help with household tasks and lifting heavy objects.
Avoid driving while in significant pain, sedated or unable to perform an emergency stop safely.
Gradually increase walking and routine activities.
Continue avoiding activities that cause significant pain or strain.
Review the wound and overall recovery if symptoms persist.
Follow local advice about driving, exercise and work.

blocks.text: Many women can gradually resume more demanding activities, but there is no single timetable appropriate for everyone.
Return to exercise, driving, sexual activity and work should depend on healing, comfort, functional ability and any complications.
OSCE tip: Avoid telling every woman that she must wait exactly six weeks before all activity. Equally, do not advise heavy lifting or strenuous exercise before adequate recovery.
Explain that there is no single mandatory date for resuming sex. The woman should feel physically comfortable, have no concerning symptoms and be ready emotionally.
Discuss vaginal dryness, particularly during breastfeeding, and the possible use of a suitable lubricant.

items.text: Fertility can return before the first postpartum period.
Breastfeeding alone does not reliably prevent pregnancy unless all lactational amenorrhoea method criteria are met.
Progestogen-only methods and implants are suitable for many postpartum women.
IUCD timing depends on the interval since delivery and clinical eligibility.
Combined hormonal contraception requires careful assessment of postpartum VTE risk and breastfeeding.

blocks.text: Offer contraceptive counselling based on the woman's preferences rather than assuming she wants a particular method.
A previous caesarean section does not automatically mean that all future deliveries must be by caesarean.

Discuss allowing adequate time for recovery before another pregnancy. Many clinicians advise aiming for an interval of approximately 18 months from delivery to the next conception when feasible, while individualising advice to maternal age, fertility considerations, medical conditions and obstetric history.
Short intervals may increase some risks, particularly after a previous caesarean section, so pregnancy planning should be discussed with the obstetric team.

content_groups.group_title: B. Mode of delivery in a future pregnancy

items.text: Planned repeat caesarean section.
Trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC), which may result in vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC).

blocks.text: Suitability depends on the type of uterine incision, previous obstetric history, current pregnancy, contraindications and the availability of emergency caesarean facilities.
The skin scar alone does not establish the type of uterine incision. The operative record is important.

blocks.title: Depending on the circumstances, previous caesarean delivery may be associated with:

items.text: Uterine scar rupture during a subsequent trial of labour.
Placenta previa and placenta accreta spectrum, especially with multiple caesarean deliveries.
Adhesions and increasing surgical complexity with repeat operations.

blocks.text: Counselling should be balanced and should not frighten the patient away from future pregnancy.
A caesarean section may be planned or may follow a stressful emergency. Some women experience disappointment, fear, grief or a sense of loss of control.

items.text: How are you feeling about your delivery?
Were there aspects of the birth that frightened or upset you?
Do you understand why the caesarean was performed?
Do you have support at home?
Have you felt persistently sad, anxious or overwhelmed?

blocks.text: Offer a debrief about the birth when appropriate. Screen for postnatal depression or trauma-related symptoms if indicated, and arrange support or referral when needed.
Before discharge after an uncomplicated caesarean section, confirm that the woman is clinically stable and that appropriate follow-up arrangements are in place.
Discharge checklist
Clinical recovery
Stable vital signs, satisfactory pain control, adequate oral intake and no unresolved complication.
Mobility and bladder
Mobilising safely and passing urine adequately after catheter removal.
Wound
Wound assessment completed, with clear dressing and wound-care instructions.
Medication
Analgesia and any indicated iron, anticoagulation or other medication explained.
Infant feeding
Breastfeeding or alternative feeding support provided; infant concerns addressed.
Safety-net advice
Warning signs of infection, haemorrhage, VTE and other complications explained.
Follow-up
Wound review, suture or staple removal if needed, and postpartum review arranged.
Future planning
Contraception, emotional wellbeing and future pregnancy planning discussed as appropriate.

subsections.subsection_title: 16. Red flags requiring urgent medical attention

blocks.text: Possible infection or wound complication
Fever, chills, spreading redness, pus, wound separation or worsening abdominal pain.
Possible haemorrhage
Heavy vaginal bleeding, fainting, severe weakness or collapse.
Possible VTE
One-sided leg swelling or pain, sudden breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood.
Possible postpartum pre-eclampsia or neurological complication
Severe or persistent headache, visual disturbance, severe upper abdominal pain, seizures or marked shortness of breath.
Tell the woman to seek emergency care immediately for severe breathlessness, chest pain, seizures, collapse or heavy bleeding. She should not wait for a scheduled postpartum appointment.

subsections.subsection_title: 17. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Why is early mobilisation important after caesarean section?
It helps reduce immobility-related VTE risk, supports bowel and bladder recovery and promotes functional recovery.
Q2. What are the common complications of caesarean section?
Haemorrhage, wound infection, endometritis, urinary tract infection, VTE, anaesthetic complications, injury to adjacent organs and complications related to the uterine scar in future pregnancies.
Q3. How do you prevent VTE after caesarean section?
Assess individual risk, encourage early mobilisation and use mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis when indicated by the local protocol.
Q4. Can a mother breastfeed after caesarean section?
Yes. Encourage breastfeeding as soon as mother and baby are stable, with assistance and positions that minimise incisional pain.
Q5. When should the wound be reviewed?
According to the discharge plan and wound closure method. Review earlier if there is increasing pain, redness, discharge, fever or wound separation.
Q6. What analgesics are suitable during breastfeeding?
Paracetamol and ibuprofen are commonly suitable when there are no contraindications. Opioids require caution, appropriate dosing and monitoring. Check each medication individually.
Q7. Can the patient have a vaginal delivery in a future pregnancy?
Potentially. TOLAC may be suitable depending on the previous uterine incision, obstetric history, current pregnancy and available emergency facilities.
Q8. Why is the operative note important?
It documents the type of uterine incision and any complications, which are important when planning future pregnancies and assessing suitability for TOLAC.
Q9. When can sexual activity resume?
When the woman feels ready, is comfortable and has no concerning symptoms. Discuss contraception and vaginal dryness where relevant.
Q10. What advice should be given about another pregnancy?
Discuss individualised pregnancy spacing, contraception, recovery, previous operative findings and early antenatal review in the next pregnancy.

items.text: Giving routine discharge advice without first assessing for complications.
Advising prolonged bed rest rather than safe early mobilisation.
Failing to assess VTE risk.
Ignoring severe or increasing pain.
Failing to explain wound infection and haemorrhage warning signs.
Advising that breastfeeding is impossible after caesarean section.
Giving blanket restrictions on driving, exercise or sexual activity without considering recovery.
Failing to discuss contraception and future pregnancy planning.
Assuming that every woman with a previous caesarean must have repeat surgery.

"I would assess the woman's postoperative recovery and ensure that there are no complications before providing discharge counselling. I would explain wound care, analgesia, early mobilisation, VTE prevention, nutrition, bladder and bowel care, and breastfeeding support. I would explain warning signs such as fever, wound discharge, heavy bleeding, unilateral leg swelling and sudden breathlessness. I would also discuss gradual return to normal activities, emotional wellbeing, contraception, appropriate pregnancy spacing and future delivery options, with clear follow-up arrangements."
